title: Summarizing Email Conversations with Clue Words
abstract: The paper proposes an email-conversation summarization framework using quotation structure and clue words to estimate sentence importance. It empirically evaluates summarization of threaded email conversations, providing direct workplace-email evidence at the single-conversation level.

admission.reason: The abstract evaluates summarization inside a single email conversation using quotation structure and sentence importance. It does not perform cross-thread or work-item aggregation, cycle-relative updating, or new/open/resolved/superseded carry-forward. This is exactly the thread-level email summarization evidence that gap-6 says is already insufficient.

title: Reinforcement Online Learning to Rank with Unbiased Reward Shaping
abstract: The paper develops an online learning-to-rank method that continuously learns from user interactions while correcting position bias through inverse-propensity-based reward shaping. Empirical evaluation on standard OLTR datasets tests effectiveness and user-experience metrics under ongoing interaction.

admission.reason: The paper continuously updates a ranker from interaction feedback and corrects position bias, but the abstract does not evaluate preference drift, changing user goals or roles, or longitudinal briefing selection. Candidate doi-10-1109-access-2022-3182390 explicitly models personalized preference drift and therefore provides the stronger evidence for F9.

title: Novelty and Redundancy Detection in Adaptive Filtering
abstract: The work extends adaptive information filtering by explicitly and separately modeling relevance and redundancy. Five redundancy measures are experimentally evaluated, providing transfer evidence for distinguishing useful new information from repeated material in a temporal stream.

admission.reason: The abstract provides useful generic relevance-versus-redundancy filtering, but it is pure novelty/redundancy control: it does not preserve unchanged-but-open important state or distinguish resolved and superseded work. Under the project boundary, novelty alone is a false friend rather than sufficient evidence for longitudinal briefing selection.

title: More Than Just a Communication System: Diversity in the Use of Electronic Mail
abstract: An empirical study of professional email users identifies distinct work-management strategies including prioritizing incoming messages, archiving information, and delegating work. The findings argue that email systems need flexible support for heterogeneous user practices and preferences.

admission.reason: The professional-email interviews establish heterogeneous work-management practices, including prioritization and delegation, but the abstract does not evaluate a briefing-selection mechanism, adaptive personalization, preference drift, or longitudinal task-state carry-forward. It is useful background for F5 but does not materially close the current high-value gaps.

title: Novelty Detection: The TREC Experience
abstract: This empirical analysis of the TREC novelty task studies identification of relevant new information in ordered topical document streams. It reports differences between human and system selections and finds that tracking novel opinions is harder than tracking events.

admission.reason: The TREC analysis studies sentence-level novelty in ordered topical streams, but the capability remains novelty detection rather than longitudinal briefing with persistence of unchanged unresolved work. Its contribution overlaps the generic novelty-transfer evidence and does not address the project's central carry-forward requirement.

title: That Escalated Quickly: An ML Framework for Alert Prioritization
abstract: The paper presents a machine-learning framework for predicting alert- and incident-level actionability in security operations. Evaluation on real-world operational data measures both false-positive suppression and preservation of actionable incidents, making it useful transfer evidence for joint false-alert and omission trade-offs in high-volume workplace alerting.

admission.reason: The real-world actionability results are relevant to false-alert suppression, but the capability substantially overlaps the broader threshold-spanning alert-prioritization evidence in verified candidate 2609.02465. Given scarce reading slots, the latter more directly supports review-capacity-sensitive evaluation across multiple datasets.

title: ConvoSumm: Conversation Summarization Benchmark and Improved Abstractive Summarization with Argument Mining
abstract: The paper creates conversation-summarization datasets spanning several domains, including email threads, and benchmarks abstractive models with automatic and human evaluation. It also evaluates argument-mining structures that explicitly represent issues, viewpoints, and assertions.

admission.reason: The abstract benchmarks conversation summarization and argument structure, including email threads, but it remains conversation-level summarization. It does not maintain a work item across conversations or successive report cycles and therefore does not resolve gap-6 or the new/open/resolved/superseded requirement.

title: Overview of the TREC 2002 Novelty Track
abstract: The TREC novelty track evaluates systems that, given an ordered set of relevant documents, identify sentences that are both relevant and novel relative to information already encountered. Thirteen groups participated in the initial evaluation.

admission.reason: This track evaluates relevant-and-novel sentence selection in ordered documents, but the abstract shows no mechanism for preserving important unchanged open state, resolving work-item lifecycle, or evaluating longitudinal briefing omissions. It is redundant with the generic novelty-detection transfer capability and is not sufficient for this round.

title: Prospective memory reminders: A laboratory investigation of initiation source and age effects
abstract: Young and older adults complete prospective-memory tasks under no-reminder, self-initiated-reminder, and experimenter-initiated-reminder conditions. The experiments test whether reminders improve remembering and whether effectiveness depends on source, task type, or age.

admission.reason: The experiments establish effects of reminder presence and initiation source on prospective-memory performance, but they do not study reminder reliability, staleness, individualized priority, or integration with importance and urgency. The 2026 reminder-reliability candidate provides a more distinctive contribution to F7 and gap-5.

title: ‘Show me more’: Incremental length summarisation using novelty detection
abstract: A user study compares summaries containing only novel sentences with incremental summaries that add contextual sentences. The experiments test whether novelty-only presentation is sufficient for relevance judgments or whether preserved context improves interpretation.

admission.reason: Despite the word 'incremental', the abstract studies increasing the length of a summary for a document and whether novel sentences need added context. It does not summarize an evolving stream across report cycles, track persistent open state, or perform longitudinal update selection. The terminology matches but the required capability does not.

title: Lexicographically-ordered constraint satisfaction problems
abstract: The paper presents a formalism that explicitly separates hard feasibility constraints from softer preferences represented by lexicographic orderings. It analyzes algorithms for finding preferred feasible solutions and relates the approach to more general soft-constraint formalisms.

admission.reason: The formalism cleanly distinguishes hard feasibility constraints from preferences, but the abstract is algorithmic/formal rather than an empirical evaluation of user-conditioned selection. The verified soft-planning-constraint candidate 2403.19795 supplies the same key distinction with an empirical preference-learning evaluation and is therefore the better F12 reading slot.

title: Experimenting with prequential variations for data stream learning evaluation
abstract: The paper empirically compares Basic Window, Sliding Window, and Fading Factors variants of prequential evaluation for data streams with concept drift. It tests how accurately each protocol reflects performance as distributions change over time and finds sliding-window prequential evaluation the strongest of the tested alternatives.

admission.reason: The paper evaluates protocols for measuring predictive performance under concept drift, not a user model that adapts to changing preferences, roles, goals, or feedback. Distributional drift terminology matches F9, but the personalization capability required by the stream is absent.

title: Classifying Action Items for Semantic Email
abstract: The Semanta system models email action items such as task assignments and meeting proposals as parts of ad-hoc workflows. A rule-based classifier is empirically evaluated, with results supporting assisted suggestions for user review rather than fully automatic classification.

admission.reason: The abstract primarily evaluates classification of email action-item speech acts and assisted annotation. Determining what an action or workflow item is belongs to the upstream action/commitment problem; it does not evaluate longitudinal selection, prioritization, cross-thread aggregation, or briefing persistence once those action items are available.

title: The nature of requests and commitments in email messages
abstract: The paper defines task-oriented requests and commitments at utterance level and validates the definitions through two manual annotation experiments on Enron email. It explicitly models requests as obligations placed on another agent and commitments as obligations accepted by an agent, including conditional cases.

admission.reason: The paper gives empirically informed definitions of requests and commitments as obligations in email, which is valuable upstream evidence for detecting responsibility. It does not evaluate how those obligations interact with softer personalized priority or reminder signals during content selection, so it does not close gap-2 and belongs primarily to the action/request extraction boundary owned upstream.

title: Detecting action-items in e-mail
abstract: The paper studies automatic detection of emails that require action or response and localization of the text expressing that request. Its formulation targets sender intent and required receiver action rather than generic topical classification.

admission.reason: The abstract detects emails requiring action or response and localizes request text. That establishes an upstream action-item signal but does not evaluate triage utility, hard-versus-soft selection, cross-thread work-item state, personalization, or longitudinal briefing behavior. Treating action detection itself as briefing prioritization would violate the project's response-obligation versus priority distinction.
